# Private-Label Purchasing<br>at [Kroger]{.accent}

::: {.lead-copy}
An analysis of household income and private-label spending, examining overall purchasing patterns and differences within Grocery categories.
:::

[Download R script](analysis.R){.btn download="kroger-private-label-analysis.R"}
:::

## Business Question

Do lower-income Kroger households allocate a larger share of their spending to private-label products than higher-income households, and is that difference concentrated in Grocery categories?

## Unit of Analysis

Our unit of analysis is the **household**.

We use households because income is measured at the household level. Each household therefore contributes one summarized private-label purchasing measure rather than households with more transactions receiving more weight.

## Defining Private-Label Purchasing

We define private-label purchasing as **private-label dollar share**:

$$
\text{Private Label Share}
=
\frac{\text{Private Label Spending}}
{\text{Total Spending}}
$$

This measures the share of a household's spending that goes to private-label products.

## Basics

Read in tidyverse and data
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
library(tidyverse)

transactions <- read_csv("transaction_data.csv")
products <- read_csv("product.csv")
demographics <- read_csv("hh_demographic.csv")
```

</details>


Join data
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
data <- transactions |>
    left_join(products, by = 'PRODUCT_ID') |>
    left_join(demographics, by = 'household_key')

glimpse(data)
```

</details>

Initial EDA
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
## Count of private and national transactions
data |>
    count(BRAND)

## Count of transactions per department
data |>
    count(DEPARTMENT, sort = TRUE)

## Count of each income groups
data |>
    count(INCOME_DESC, sort = TRUE)

## Count of transactions with demographic info
data |>
    summarise(
        total_rows = n(),
        rows_with_income = sum(!is.na(INCOME_DESC)),
        percent_with_income = mean(!is.na(INCOME_DESC)) * 100
    )
```

</details>

Create new variable to track only private label product sales
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
data <- data |>
    mutate(
        private_sales = if_else(
            BRAND == 'Private',
            SALES_VALUE, 0
            )
    )
```

</details>

## Analysis

Rearrange data to household granularity
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
household_data <- data |>
    filter(!is.na(INCOME_DESC)) |>
    group_by(household_key, INCOME_DESC) |>
    summarise(
        total_sales = sum(SALES_VALUE, na.rm = TRUE),
        private_sales = sum(private_sales, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = 'drop'
    ) |>
        mutate(
            private_share = private_sales / total_sales
        )

glimpse(household_data)
summary(household_data$private_share)
```

</details>

Private label purchases by income groups
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
household_data |>
    group_by(INCOME_DESC) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        median_private_share = median(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_private_share = sd(private_share, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
        arrange(desc(mean_private_share))
```

</details>


Distribution of private label dollar share
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
ggplot(household_data, aes(x = private_share)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
    labs(
        title = 'Distribution of Household Private Label Dollar Share',
        x = 'Private Label Dollar Share',
        y = 'Number of Households'
    )
```

</details>

Private-label dollar share by income group
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
ggplot(household_data, aes(x = INCOME_DESC, y = private_share)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
        title = 'Private Label Dollar Share by Household Income',
        x = 'Income Group',
        y = 'Private Label Dollar Share '
    )
```

</details>

Income group summary
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
income_summary <- household_data |>
    group_by(INCOME_DESC) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        median_private_share = median(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_private_share = sd(private_share, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
        arrange(desc(mean_private_share))

income_summary
```

</details>

Now you have an actual finding to work with — and it’s more interesting than a simple “lower income buys more private label” story.

Your descriptive results show:

Overall mean private label dollar share: 27.7%
Median: 26.9%
100–124K is highest observed group at 30.2%
Several lower income groups are around 28–29%

The highest-income groups are much lower:

- 150–174K: 22.7%
- 175–199K: 22.0%
- 250K+: 16.6%
- 200–249K: 16.3%

Last few groups have very small sample sizes, (especially 200–249K with only 5 households). Collapse in broader groups.

Establish broader groups
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
household_data <- household_data |>
    mutate(
        income_group = case_when(
            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "Under 15K",
                "15-24K",
                "25-34K",
                "35-49K"
            ) ~ "Below $50K",

            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "50-74K",
                "75-99K"
            ) ~ "$50K-$99K",

            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "100-124K",
                "125-149K",
                "150-174K",
                "175-199K",
                "200-249K",
                "250K+"
            ) ~ "$100K+"
        )
    )
```

</details>

Summarize new groups
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
income_group_summary <- household_data |>
    group_by(income_group) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share),
        median_private_share = median(private_share),
        sd_private_share = sd(private_share)
    )

income_group_summary
```

</details>

New plot
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
ggplot(
    household_data,
    aes(x = income_group, y = private_share)
) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(

```

## ANOVA

Welch's one way ANOVA best because of unequal sizes and different standard deviations
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
oneway.test(
    private_share ~ income_group,
    data = household_data,
    var.equal = FALSE
)
```

</details>

Welch ANOVA Result:

- F = 5.7469
- p = 0.003509


Average private-label dollar share is not the same across all three income groups.

Your grouped means are:

- Below $50K: 28.9%
- $50K–$99K: 27.2%
-  $100K+: 25.0%

So broad pattern is: **Private-label dollar share decreases as household income rises.**

ANOVA only tells shows at least one group differs, not which pairs differ.

Next step is a pairwise follow-up with Welch pairwise t-tests with a multiple-comparison adjustment
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
pairwise.t.test(
    household_data$private_share,
    household_data$income_group,
    p.adjust.method = "bonferroni",
    pool.sd = FALSE
)
```

</details>

Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise p-values:

- $50K–$99K vs $100K+: p = 0.256
- Below $50K vs $100K+: p = 0.004
- Below $50K vs $50K–$99K: p = 0.173

Only statistically significant pair **Below $50K vs $100K+**

And the observed mean difference is 0.039 (0.289 - 0.250)

Households below $50K spend about 3.9 percentage points more of their total spending on private-label products than households earning $100K+. The middle-income group is not significantly different from either side after the Bonferroni adjustment.

**Private-label dollar share differs across income groups overall, but the clearest difference is between households below $50K and households earning $100K or more.**

Quantify key difference with confidence interval
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
t.test(
    private_share ~ income_group,
    data = household_data |>
        filter(income_group %in% c("Below $50K", "$100K+"))
)
```

</details>

- $100K+ mean PL share: 25.05%
- Below $50K mean PL share: 28.88%
- Difference: about 3.83 percentage points
- 95% CI for $100K+ − Below $50K: -6.15 to -1.51 percentage points
- p = 0.00133

Households earning below $50K spend about 3.8 percentage points more of their total dollars on private label products than households earning $100K or more. The 95% confidence interval suggests the true gap is roughly 1.5 to 6.2 percentage points.

Is income gap concentrated within certain departments
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
department_data <- data |>
    filter(!is.na(INCOME_DESC)) |>
    mutate(
        income_group = case_when(
            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "Under 15K",
                "15-24K",
                "25-34K",
                "35-49K"
            ) ~ "Below $50K",

            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "50-74K",
                "75-99K"
            ) ~ "$50K-$99K",

            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "100-124K",
                "125-149K",
                "150-174K",
                "175-199K",
                "200-249K",
                "250K+"
            ) ~ "$100K+"
        )
    ) |>
    filter(income_group %in% c("Below $50K", "$100K+")) |>
    group_by(household_key, income_group, DEPARTMENT) |>
    summarise(
        total_sales = sum(SALES_VALUE, na.rm = TRUE),
        private_sales = sum(private_sales, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
        private_share = private_sales / total_sales
    )
```

</details>

Summarize by department
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
department_summary <- department_data |>
    group_by(DEPARTMENT, income_group) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

department_summary
```

</details>

Not a good idea to use all 44 departments. Some departments have tiny samples and mechanically extreme shares, like AUTOMOTIVE = 1.00 with only 7–11 households. Those aren’t very useful for the business story.

GROCERY is by far the largest department in the transaction data, and gives a good “where”

Check grocery
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
department_summary |>
    filter(DEPARTMENT == "GROCERY")
```

</details>

Compare Below 50k and 100k+ Does the overall income difference in private-label purchasing persist specifically within Grocery?
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
t.test(
    private_share ~ income_group,
    data = department_data |>
        filter(DEPARTMENT == "GROCERY")
)
```

</details>

Find biggest commodity categories within grocery
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
top_grocery_commodities <- data |>
    filter(
        DEPARTMENT == "GROCERY",
        !is.na(COMMODITY_DESC)
    ) |>
    group_by(COMMODITY_DESC) |>
    summarise(
        total_sales = sum(SALES_VALUE, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(desc(total_sales))

top_grocery_commodities
```

</details>

Among households with reported income, lower income households devoted about 7 percentage points more of their Grocery spending to private label products than households earning $100K+, with the estimated gap plausibly around 4.7–9.4 percentage points.

Figure out which Grocery categories are driving that difference
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
top_categories <- c(
    "SOFT DRINKS",
    "FLUID MILK PRODUCTS",
    "CHEESE",
    "FRZN MEAT/MEAT DINNERS",
    "BAG SNACKS"
)
```

</details>

Household summary per category
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
commodity_data <- data |>
    filter(
        DEPARTMENT == "GROCERY",
        COMMODITY_DESC %in% top_categories,
        !is.na(INCOME_DESC)
    ) |>
    mutate(
        income_group = case_when(
            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "Under 15K",
                "15-24K",
                "25-34K",
                "35-49K"
            ) ~ "Below $50K",

            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "100-124K",
                "125-149K",
                "150-174K",
                "175-199K",
                "200-249K",
                "250K+"
            ) ~ "$100K+"
        )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(income_group)) |>
    group_by(
        household_key,
        income_group,
        COMMODITY_DESC
    ) |>
    summarise(
        total_sales = sum(SALES_VALUE, na.rm = TRUE),
        private_sales = sum(private_sales, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
        private_share = private_sales / total_sales
    )
```

</details>

Average private-label dollar share within that category among households that purchased something in that category.
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
commodity_summary <- commodity_data |>
    group_by(COMMODITY_DESC, income_group) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share),
        median_private_share = median(private_share),
        .groups = "drop"
    )

commodity_summary
```

</details>

Test whether those category gaps are statistically distinguishable.
<details>
<summary>View R code</summary>

```r
commodity_tests <- commodity_data |>
    group_by(COMMODITY_DESC) |>
    group_modify(~ {
        test <- t.test(
            private_share ~ income_group,
            data = .x
        )

        tibble(
            difference = unname(
                test$estimate["mean in group Below $50K"] -
                test$estimate["mean in group $100K+"]
            ),
            conf_low = -test$conf.int[2],
            conf_high = -test$conf.int[1],
            p_value = test$p.value
        )
    }) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(
        p_adjusted = p.adjust(p_value, method = "bonferroni")
    )

commodity_tests
```

</details>

Lower-income households allocate a larger share of Grocery spending to private label, with particularly pronounced differences in soft drinks, cheese, and fluid milk.

## Recommendation

Kroger should prioritize private-label positioning and promotion for lower-income households in high-volume Grocery categories where the income gap in private-label purchasing is strongest.

The clearest opportunities in this analysis are:

- Cheese
- Soft drinks
- Fluid milk products

Kroger should also investigate why $100K+ households show lower private-label adoption in these categories.

## Limitations

- Income is only available for a subset of households.
- This is observational analysis, so income should not be interpreted as causing private-label purchasing.
- Household composition, shopping frequency, store location, and assortment could also contribute to the observed differences.
- The commodity analysis examines only five high-sales Grocery categories.

## Conclusion

Private-label dollar share differs across income groups. The clearest difference is between households below $50K and households earning $100K or more.

That gap becomes larger within Grocery and is most evident among the selected high-volume categories in cheese, soft drinks, and fluid milk products.
